```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  eval = crywolf:::.has_cmdstan()   # chunks that need Stan run only with CmdStan
)
```

Automated detectors, such as the acoustic classifiers that scan thousands of
hours of recordings, make two kinds of mistakes: they miss calls, and they
label other sounds as the target species. Occupancy models deal with the
first kind by repeating surveys, but false positives inflate occupancy and,
worse, can distort the effects of environmental covariates. **crywolf** fits
the multiple-methods false-positive occupancy model of Miller et al. (2011),
in which a subset of detections is checked by an expert, and helps you ask
whether the correction is good enough for your design.

## The design

At every site, the classifier scans several recordings (the *automated*
occasions). At a subset of sites, someone also listens to a few clips and
records whether the species was really there (the *verified* occasions).
Verified detections are certain, so they tell the model how often the
classifier is wrong.

## Installation

crywolf fits its models with [CmdStan](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/)
through **cmdstanr**. Install both once:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("cmdstanr", repos = c("https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev",
                                       getOption("repos")))
cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()
remotes::install_github("diogoprov/crywolf")
```

```{r load, eval = TRUE}
library(crywolf)
```

## Your data

`fp_data()` takes three tables in long format: the automated detections (one
row per site and occasion), the sites with their covariates, and, optionally,
the verified detections. Here we simulate data instead, with a false-positive
rate that rises along a gradient correlated with the occupancy covariate, as
happens when a soundalike species becomes commoner where the target is rare.

```{r simulate, eval = TRUE}
sim <- simulate_fp(nsite = 300, nocc = 20, psi = 0.5, b1 = -0.8,
                   p11 = 0.6, p10 = 0.05,
                   conf_effect = 1.5, conf_cor = 0.7,
                   frac_verified = 0.3, seed = 2026)
sim
head(sim$data$auto)
head(sim$data$sites)
```

If your detections are in site-by-occasion matrices, as in **unmarked**,
`fp_data_wide()` builds the same object.

## Fitting the model

`fp_occu()` takes a formula for each process. With `fp = ~ 1` the
false-positive rate is constant, which is what most applications assume.

```{r fit-constant}
m_const <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, det = ~ 1, fp = ~ 1,
                   random_recorder = FALSE, seed = 1)
m_const
```

The true occupancy slope is −0.8. Because the false positives track a
gradient correlated with `x`, the constant-rate model attributes part of the
false positives to the occupancy process, and the slope is pulled towards
zero. The site where the classifier is fooled most looks like a site where
the species is present.

The practical remedy is to let the false-positive rate depend on the
occupancy covariate, which you always have:

```{r fit-x}
m_x <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, det = ~ 1, fp = ~ x,
               random_recorder = FALSE, seed = 1)
coef(m_const, "occ")
coef(m_x, "occ")
```

and, if you have measured a covariate of whatever fools the classifier,
adding it as well. In a simulation we know that variable, `w`, so we can fit
the generating model as a positive control:

```{r fit-w}
m_w <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, det = ~ 1, fp = ~ w,
               random_recorder = FALSE, seed = 1)
summary(m_w)
```

## Comparing models

The pointwise log-likelihood is computed per site, with the latent state
marginalized, so `loo()` gives leave-one-site-out cross-validation.

```{r loo}
loo::loo_compare(list(constant = loo(m_const), fp_x = loo(m_x), fp_w = loo(m_w)))
```

## Predictions

`predict()` returns the occupancy probability, or the false-positive rate,
with credible intervals.

```{r predict}
nd <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 2, by = 1))
predict(m_x, newdata = nd, process = "occ")
predict(m_x, newdata = nd, process = "fp")
```

## Covariates on detection and recorders

The true-detection formula accepts observation covariates (columns of
`auto`) and site covariates, and `random_recorder = TRUE` adds a random
intercept per recorder.

```{r det, eval = FALSE}
fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, det = ~ bio + aci, fp = ~ x,
        random_recorder = TRUE)
```

## Is the correction calibrated for my design?

A single fit cannot tell you whether the credible intervals are honest.
`fp_calibrate()` and `fp_verification_curve()` answer that by simulation; see
`vignette("calibration", package = "crywolf")`.

## References

Miller, D. A., Nichols, J. D., McClintock, B. T., Grant, E. H. C., Bailey,
L. L., & Weir, L. A. (2011). Improving occupancy estimation when two types of
observational error occur: non-detection and species misidentification.
*Ecology*, 92, 1422–1428. https://doi.org/10.1890/10-1396.1
